title: Alpha and transparency
learningObjectives: Explain alpha and transparency and apply it correctly in a small CSS example.

understand.concept: Alpha describes how opaque a colour is when it is composited with what is behind it. In modern CSS colour functions, alpha is commonly written after a slash as a number from 0 to 1 or a percentage. Zero is fully transparent; one is fully opaque.
understand.whyItMatters: A transparent colour allows the backdrop to contribute to the final displayed pixel. The result depends on both foreground and background colours. Transparent does not mean the element itself disappears.
understand.analogy: Imagine a coloured transparent sheet over a page. The page remains present and affects what you see through the sheet; the final appearance depends on both layers.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy helps build intuition, but the browser follows the CSS specifications and computed-style rules rather than human intentions.

explain.narrative: The background gradient remains visible through the overlay. Change 50% to 15% and 85%.

examples.explanation: The background gradient remains visible through the overlay. Change 50% to 15% and 85%.
examples.expectedOutput: A browser-rendered demonstration of the CSS concept described in the lesson.

practise.guidedTask: Create two overlays with different alpha values over the same background and describe the difference.
hints: Change one CSS value at a time and observe the result.
Use browser developer tools to inspect the computed value.
Keep meaningful content in HTML; use CSS for presentation.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to learn the effect of a CSS value?
options: Change one value and inspect the rendered result
Add unrelated declarations until it looks right
Assume every browser calculates styles identically in every context
questions.answer: Change one value and inspect the rendered result
questions.explanation: Controlled experiments make it easier to connect a CSS declaration with its visible effect.
